profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between the nurse-scientist principal investigator and the regional home-care operations lead for a multicenter pilot study on compression treatment for leg ulcers delivered in community home-care programs. The team is using a pilot-study framework modeled on the PReP approach to prepare a 12-week pragmatic pilot before a larger definitive randomized controlled trial. The agenda is to align on startup tasks for three home-care branches: how screening will be tracked, when baseline data will be collected, what counts toward the recruitment goal, how staff training will be rolled out, and who owns each activity. The expected outcome is a practical startup plan with assigned responsibilities and a launch timeline that both participants believe is settled.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Principal Investigator and Wound Care Nurse Scientist
members.expertise: Pilot study methodology, community wound care research, pragmatic trial design
members.background: Elena is a university-affiliated nurse researcher who has led several small feasibility studies in chronic wound care and is adapting a pilot-study planning framework for this leg ulcer compression trial with community partners.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to generate clean feasibility evidence that will satisfy funders and ethics reviewers for a larger multicenter trial, and she is worried that operational shortcuts will make the pilot look stronger than it really is or create unusable feasibility data.
hidden_assumptions: A screening log in a pilot study should include every potentially eligible leg-ulcer referral seen during the study window, not just patients clinicians choose to approach.
The 'baseline visit' is the research assessment completed after consent and immediately before randomization, even if it happens on the same day as routine care.
A recruitment target refers to randomized participants because pilot feasibility depends on whether participants actually reach allocation.
Study training means every nurse who may deliver protocol-related care completes the formal webinar and documentation practice before the first participant is enrolled.

members.name: Jason Miller
members.expertise: Community nursing operations, branch staffing, wound program implementation
members.background: Jason oversees clinical operations for three home-care branches and has experience rolling out new wound-care programs across decentralized nursing teams, with a strong focus on keeping documentation burdens and startup delays manageable.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to feel operationally light enough that branch managers stay engaged and frontline nurses do not see it as disruptive, and he is concerned that overly research-heavy procedures will delay launch and reduce clinical buy-in.
hidden_assumptions: A screening log should capture only patients staff genuinely consider for study approach, because documenting every leg-ulcer referral is an unnecessary operational burden.
The 'baseline visit' is the patient's first routine home-care wound assessment, since that is when the most clinically meaningful starting measurements are already documented.
A recruitment commitment is met when eligible patients consent, even if randomization is delayed by ABI testing, physician sign-off, or other routine steps outside branch control.
Training is adequately completed when each branch wound champion is briefed and then informally cascades the protocol to staff as cases arise.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the screening log
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they will keep a 'screening log' at each branch.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a log of all leg-ulcer referrals reviewed during the pilot period, including patients found ineligible or never approached, so feasibility of identification and eligibility can be quantified.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a log only for patients nurses actively consider approaching for the study after an informal clinical pre-filter, so the burden stays realistic for branch staff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because 'screening log' is a standard research phrase, both assume the other shares the obvious scope; the difference concerns the outer boundary of routine documentation rather than a headline design choice.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss collecting measures at the 'baseline visit' or 'first visit.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the post-consent, pre-randomization study baseline assessment tied to the trial timeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the patient's first routine home-care intake visit, which may occur before consent and before randomization logistics are completed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In community care, the first clinical visit often feels naturally equivalent to baseline, so each person hears the same phrase and maps it to the visit most familiar in their own workflow without realizing it is a different event.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts toward the recruitment target
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree on a 'recruitment target of 24 in three months.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 24 participants actually randomized across the three branches within the pilot recruitment window.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 24 eligible patients consented or enrolled into the startup pipeline, even if some are not randomized within that window because ancillary steps are pending.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'recruitment target' sounds fully specified in ordinary project talk, and neither participant expects a hidden distinction between consented and randomized counts unless enrollment problems later appear.

misalignment_points.topic: How site training will be completed
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the branches can launch once the 'training package' is done.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means all nurses who may deliver study-related compression care or collect study forms complete a formal webinar plus brief documentation practice before any participant is enrolled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the wound champion at each branch attends the briefing and then informally trains nurses on the job as eligible cases arise.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Training is treated as an implementation detail rather than a debated design issue, so the conversation easily stays at the level of 'getting training out' without surfacing assumptions about audience, completeness, or timing.

turns.inner_thought: I need this meeting to land concrete startup decisions that will produce defensible feasibility data, not just a soft operational agreement. The PReP-style pilot framework only helps if we can quantify identification, eligibility, consent, randomization, and adherence cleanly across all three branches. If we gloss over definitions now, we'll pay for it when the ethics board or funder asks what actually happened during the pilot window.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Jason. My goal today is to map out startup for the three-branch leg ulcer pilot using the pilot-study framework and leave with clear owners, clear timelines, and a practical launch plan for July.

turns.inner_thought: The branch managers are onside as long as this doesn't feel like a university project dropped on top of regular care. I need to keep startup light. If the training package can go through the wound champions first, we can avoid holding up launch while trying to get every nurse formally trained in advance.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From the operations side, the branch managers are supportive, and I think the sites should be ready to move once the training package is done.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I need the screening log framed early. For me that means every leg-ulcer referral reviewed during the study window, including those found ineligible and those never approached, otherwise we won't know whether recruitment struggled because patients weren't identified, weren't eligible, or weren't approached. It has to be simple enough for branch use but complete enough to support a real feasibility analysis.
turns.utterance: Great. One thing I'd like in place from day one is a simple screening log at each branch so we can see the full flow during the pilot window and understand where patients are being lost.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with a screening log as long as it's limited to the patients nurses genuinely consider for approach. If we ask teams to document every leg-ulcer referral that passes through the branch, they'll see this as extra surveillance work and stop engaging. Better to keep it tight and realistic for routine workflow.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree. If we keep the screening log straightforward and have nurses note the patients they actually screen for the study, it should stay manageable in the normal home-care workflow.

turns.inner_thought: I need the baseline visit anchored to the trial timeline: after consent and immediately before randomization. That's when wound size, pain, and compression history need to be captured in a consistent study way. If people start pulling baseline values from earlier clinical contacts, we'll have timing drift and unusable baseline data for the definitive trial planning.
turns.utterance: On data collection, I'd like the baseline visit to include wound size, pain score, and compression history before randomization so the pilot lines up with the larger trial procedures.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine because most of those fields are already captured at the patient's first routine home visit. If baseline can ride along with the intake assessment nurses already do, we won't create a separate research visit or duplicate charting. That's exactly the kind of fit-to-workflow the branches want.
turns.utterance: I think that can work well. Most of that is already captured at the first visit, so the baseline visit should fit pretty naturally into the intake assessment nurses are already doing.

turns.inner_thought: Now the recruitment benchmark. For the pilot to say anything meaningful, the target has to be 24 randomized participants in three months, not just people who sign consent and then stall in pre-randomization steps. Funders will want evidence that the allocation pathway works in community care, not just that patients are initially willing.
turns.utterance: In terms of feasibility, if we can reach a recruitment target of 24 in three months across the three branches, that will give us a solid signal for the definitive trial.

turns.inner_thought: Twenty-four sounds doable if each branch can get about two patients a month into the pipeline. Some will naturally be waiting on ABI testing or physician confirmation, but I would still count those as recruited because the branch has done its part. I need a target the managers feel they can actually hit without owning delays outside their control.
turns.utterance: That sounds achievable from my side. Each branch should be able to bring in about two recruits a month, even if some cases are still waiting on ABI testing or physician confirmation.

turns.inner_thought: I should restate the training expectation. For me, the training package is not complete until every nurse who may deliver protocol compression care or touch study forms has done the webinar and a brief documentation practice before the first participant is enrolled. Otherwise we risk inconsistent care delivery and messy forms from the very first case.
turns.utterance: And just to keep implementation clean, before the first patient is enrolled I'd want all participating nurses to complete the webinar and practice the study documentation so data collection is consistent from day one.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle this through the branch wound champions. If each champion gets the training package and rolls it out informally as cases come up, we can preserve the July start. I don't want to signal resistance, but I also don't want to commit the branches to pulling every possible nurse into a formal session before the first patient.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll ask each branch wound champion to handle the training rollout and keep the July startup timeline moving, and we can track progress branch by branch.
